title: The Bacchae
author: Euripides
openingText: Dionysus. (Dionysus enters.) I have arrived here in Thebes: Dionysus, the son of Zeus, whom Semelê, Kadmus' daughter, bore when lightning drove her into labour. I have exchanged my divine appearance for a human one and stand beside the springs of Dirkê and the waters of Ismenus. Near the palace I can see my mother's grave, where the thunderbolt struck her. The wreckage of her house still smoulders with Zeus's fire, the enduring mark of Hera's violence against my mother. Kadmus has rightly made this ground, his daughter's burial place, a sanctuary. I myself have enclosed it in the thick green growth of vines. I left the gold-rich fields of Lydia and Phrygia and travelled across the sun-scorched Persian country, past Bactrian fortresses and the storm-beaten land of Media, onwards through blessed Araby and all Asia beside the salt sea, with its crowds of lofty-towered cities where Hellenes live among foreign peoples. Of the cities of Hellas, this is the first I visit. In those other countries I established my dances and ceremonies to reveal myself to people as a God. Here in Hellas, Thebes was the first place I stirred with my triumphant cry, dressing her in fawnskin and putting the ivy-covered thyrsus into her hand. For my mother's sisters—shame upon them!—declared that Zeus had never fathered Dionysus. Semelê, they said, had slept with a mortal and blamed Zeus for her own lust, a clever deception devised by Kadmus! That was why, they boasted, Zeus killed the lying woman who claimed him as her lover. So I have driven them from home with the sting of madness. They live distracted in the mountains, compelled to wear the clothing of my celebrations. Every woman of Kadmus' people, every one, I drove raving out of her house. They sit among Kadmus' sons beneath green pine trees on exposed rocks. Thebes must learn, however unwillingly, what it means to remain outside my sacred mysteries. I must defend Semelê's honour, revealing to mortals the God she bore to Zeus. Now Kadmus has handed his crown and royal authority to Pentheus, another daughter's son. In attacking me he fights heaven itself: he excludes me from his offerings of wine and leaves my name out of his prayers. I will therefore demonstrate my divinity to him and to all Thebes. Once I have triumphed here, I will move to another country and reveal myself there. If the angry Thebans take up weapons to drive their Bacchants from the mountains, I will lead my Maenads against them in battle. That is why I have assumed a mortal body and changed my appearance to a man's. Women who left Tmolus, Lydia's wall of rock, my company of revellers whom I brought from foreign homes to share my travels and my rest, raise the cymbals invented by great Mother Rhea and myself, the instruments of Phrygian towns. Surround Pentheus' royal palace and strike them so that Kadmus' city may witness it. I will go into Kithairon's valleys, where my Bacchanals are living, and dance with them there. (He leaves. The Chorus enters, waving thyrsus-wands and striking their timbrels.)
about:
Dionysus comes to Thebes in human disguise and demands recognition as a god. Pentheus, the city's king, tries to suppress his rites and imprison the stranger who teaches them. Their confrontation draws in the royal family, the women on the mountain and the chorus of Dionysus's followers.

The play moves between arguments outside the palace, choral songs and two long reports from the mountain. Listen for the difference between what a speaker believes and what the audience has already heard. Divine power is real within the action, but the characters still dispute whether its punishment is just.

This modern edition follows the supplied English translation by Arthur S. Way. Its eleven reading sections retain the source's paragraph structure, including the abrupt transition into Dionysus's final speech. The chorus sometimes speaks as one person. Names and ritual titles can vary: Dionysus is also called Bacchus, Bromius, Evius and Iacchus. The thyrsus is the ritual staff carried by his followers. The English source adapts wordplay on Pentheus's name; the Danish rendering conveys the threat without claiming a Danish etymology.

angleCards.title: Who controls the encounter?
angleCards.text: Follow the commands, warnings and invitations exchanged by Pentheus and the stranger. Notice when their apparent balance of power changes.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow how power changes hands in the dialogue.

angleCards.title: Listening to the chorus
angleCards.text: The chorus celebrates release from fear but also calls for violent revenge. Ask how its songs shape your response to the action.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to distinguish the chorus's beliefs from my own judgement of the play.

angleCards.title: What the messengers see
angleCards.text: The two long reports describe events away from the palace. Compare what the witnesses observe with what Pentheus expects to hear.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare eyewitness accounts with the assumptions made by other characters.

angleCards.title: Recognition and responsibility
angleCards.text: In the final section, brief questions slowly change Agave's understanding. Follow what she remembers, what she sees and whom each speaker holds responsible.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the recognition scene closely and consider responsibility under divine compulsion.

cast.name: Dionysus
cast.description: Son of Zeus and Semele. He comes to Thebes to establish his rites and confront those who deny his divinity.

cast.name: Pentheus
cast.description: Son of Agave and Echion, and grandson of Kadmus. He opposes Dionysus and wants to discover what the women are doing on the mountain.

cast.name: Kadmus
cast.description: Father of Semele and Agave, and grandfather of Pentheus. He joins Teiresias in honouring Dionysus and urges the king to do the same.

cast.name: Agave
cast.description: One of Kadmus's daughters. She is among the women whom Dionysus has driven from Thebes to the mountain.

cast.name: Teiresias
cast.description: An elderly prophet who argues for honouring Dionysus and prepares to join his dances with Kadmus.

cast.name: The chorus
cast.description: Women from Asia who have accompanied the god. Their songs and exchanges respond to events outside the palace.

cast.name: The herdsman and messenger
cast.description: They report what they have seen away from the palace. Their accounts bring the mountain's events into the action on stage.

whyItMatters.title: Power and justice
whyItMatters.body: Pentheus's authority and Dionysus's power collide. Their confrontation leaves a question the characters themselves raise: does a real god's power make every act of revenge just?

whyItMatters.title: Seeing and understanding
whyItMatters.body: Disguise, mistaken identity and recognition shape the action. The play repeatedly separates what people see from what they understand.
